sentences.text: Iberosuchus, which translates to "Iberian crocodile," is an extinct genus of mesoeucrocodylian sebecosuchian that lived in Western Europe during the Eocene.
This genus contains only a single species, I. macrodon, a name meaning "large-toothed."
The animal possessed ziphodont teeth, a term for crowns that are laterally compressed and curved at the tips, with denticles along their edges.
Its dorsal osteoderms were elongated from front to back and featured a central keel, sometimes forming a cross shape with accessory processes in smaller specimens.
These bony plates displayed rough ornamentations but lacked pits or cupules.
The skull exhibited a worm-like texture, while the snout or lower jaw was deep and included a spoon-like shelf.
Remains from Portugal were first described in 1975 by Antunes as a sebecosuchian crocodilian.
The initial cranial remains were excavated from the Feligueira Grande Formation in the Leiria District of Portugal.
Later, Robert Carroll reclassified the genus as a baurusuchid in 1988.
In 1996, Ortega and colleagues extended the known range of Iberosuchus to France by reassigning the fragmentary species Atacisaurus crassiproratus to it.
Unlike modern crocodilians, Iberosuchus was a terrestrial animal rather than an aquatic one.
It was a predator that lived on land instead of in water.
Iberosuchus has synonyms including Atacisaurus, named by Astre in 1931, and Isselosaurus, named by Filhol in 1888.
Iberosuchus lived between 56 and 33.9 million years ago during the Ypresian to Priabonian stages.
A mandibular element was found in Caenes, Spain, dating to the Bartonian age, roughly 44 to 39 million years ago.
A snout fragment was discovered in the Tosalet del Morral of Lerida province, Spain, dating to the Lutetian age.
The oldest fossils found at the Aumelas site in France date back to the mid-Lutetian age, specifically MP 13.
Fossils from the Robiac site in France date to the Bartonian age, MP 16.
